title: The difference between a redesign and a new offer
metaTitle: Redesign the site, or change the offer
excerpt: A redesign keeps the offer and changes how a stranger understands it. If the offer itself changed, rewrite the sentences before anyone opens a layout file.
alt: A clothing shop with racks, rope-hung industrial lamps, and a mirror, the same goods in a room that can be redesigned without changing what is for sale.
caption: Racks, lamps, and a mirror. A redesign changes the room. A new offer changes what is for sale. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How can you tell a redesign from a new offer?
faqs.answer: List the claims on the current site: who it is for, what they buy, and what happens next. If those nouns survive, you are redesigning how the offer is understood. If the nouns changed, rewrite the sentences before you change the layout.

faqs.question: What is a redesign allowed to change?
faqs.answer: The order of the story, the proof, the type, the number of templates, and the speed and stability of the shipped page. The promise a past customer would recognize should stay. Hiding the only working path behind a new form makes the business harder to buy.

faqs.question: What if only the price changed?
faqs.answer: A new way of charging is a new offer, even if the screens look familiar. Explain the shape of the price before you redraw packages in new boxes. A contact line with no shape is the old door, repainted.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A redesign keeps the offer and changes how a stranger understands it. The product, the price logic, and the customer stay. The structure, the type, the proof, and the path get clearer. A website redesign vs new offer is the fork you have to name before anyone opens a layout file.

If the offer itself changed, rewrite the sentences first. A new layout will only varnish the old pitch, and the old pitch is now a lie you paid to illustrate.

## How to tell which one you are in

Read the homepage you have, out loud, and mark every claim. Who it is for. What they buy. What it costs, or how the cost is decided. What happens next. Then write the claims you wish were on the site next quarter.

If the nouns survived, you are in a redesign. The shop still sells the same goods. The software still does the same job. The studio still offers the same kind of engagement. You are changing hierarchy, proof, speed, and the order of the story.

If the nouns changed, you are in a new offer. You used to sell projects and now you sell a subscription. You used to serve clinics and now you serve hospitals. You used to ship a physical good and now you sell a service with a shop on the side. The sentences have to change before the grid does.

A mixed case is common and still decidable. The offer is the same and one audience is new. Redesign the core, and give the new audience a path. Do not let the new audience's language replace the payer's language on the first screen unless the payer has actually changed.

Hanabi would ask for those two lists in the first working session. The design tools come after. Figma is the right place to try structure once the sentences are stable. It is the wrong place to discover that the company has changed its mind.

## What a redesign is allowed to change

Change the order. Lead with the job, then the proof, then the action. Many older sites lead with an origin story because that was the fashion when they launched. A redesign can retire the origin story to the about page without retiring the company.

Change the proof. Replace a row of logos with one project and a constraint. Down the Cove, an ecommerce migration and redesign, is a public example of this kind of work: the shop had to be understood again, not reinvented as a different business. Thomas Bewick kept a heritage craft and made it readable as a modern editorial site. The offer of the underlying work stayed. The page caught up.

Change the type, the space, and the color if the current system is hard to read or hard to extend. Keep the name and the recognizable mark unless the mark itself blocks the offer. A redesign can be visually quiet and still be a redesign. Clients sometimes ask for "more energy" when they need fewer competing buttons.

Change the template count. Ten slightly different page types can become four. That is often the most valuable part of a redesign, and the least photogenic. Write it into the scope as pages and states, so it does not get traded away for a more dramatic hero.

Change the speed and the stability of the page. People feel a redesign that jumps, loads late, or shifts under their thumb, even if they never say those words. web.dev describes the Core Web Vitals as loading, interactivity, and visual stability: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint at 200 milliseconds or less, and cumulative layout shift at 0.1 or less, judged at the 75th percentile of visits. A redesign that ignores the shipped page and only polishes a picture has not finished.

## What has to stay, or you have started a different project

The promise stays. If you still do the work, say so in words a past customer would recognize. A redesign that makes you sound like a different category will confuse the people who were about to refer you.

The proof that is still true stays. Do not delete the only project a buyer can recognize because the photograph feels dated. Recrop it, rewrite the caption, and keep the fact. You can add better proof beside it.

The path to start stays, unless it was genuinely broken. A phone number, a booking link, a cart. A redesign that hides the only working path behind a new "get in touch" form has made the business harder to buy. Measure that before you celebrate the type.

The name stays, unless the name is the problem you actually set out to solve. Renaming is a brand project. It wants its own decision, its own files, and a plan for the old name. Folding a rename into a homepage refresh is how both arrive half-done.

Google's guidance on title links is a practical test of whether you stayed or strayed. The title element and the main heading should describe the page you have now. If you redesigned and the offer is the same, the title can get clearer and more specific. If the visible page still says the old offer because the sentences were never rewritten, a prettier template will not save the search result. Google may rewrite a title that does not match the page. Give it a title that already matches.

## If the offer changed, stop drawing

Write the new offer in a few sentences a stranger can repeat. Who it is for. What they get. What they do next. What you no longer do. Read it to someone who knew the old company. If they say "so you still do the old thing," the sentences are not done.

List what the new offer makes obsolete. Pages, packages, a pricing story, a feature you will not carry forward. Those pages should be redirected or rewritten, not skinned. A skin on an obsolete page is how a sales call starts with an apology.

Then, and only then, look at structure. The new offer might need a different first screen, a different proof, a different form. That is a site project with a strategy in front of it. Calling it a redesign will set the wrong budget and the wrong expectation of how much copy has to move.

Pricing is the usual tell. If the way you charge changed, the site cannot lead with the old packages in new boxes. Explain the shape of the price, even if you cannot publish a number. A contact line with no shape is the old door, repainted.

Voice changes more slowly than an offer, and it should. You can say a new thing without adopting a new personality every time the market shifts. Keep the type and the tone. Change the nouns. Wabisabi did not need to become loud to be specific. Ballarat Box Sports did not need to become a software brand to be clear. Specificity is the move. A costume is the trap.

## A simple way to brief the work

Write one paragraph at the top of the brief: "The offer is unchanged. We are changing how it is understood." Or: "The offer has changed. Here are the new sentences. The layout follows."

Under that, list pages to keep, pages to rewrite, and pages to retire. Attach the sentences. A designer who receives a brief with no sentences will design the old offer in better type, because the old offer is what the current site contains. That is not a failure of taste. It is a failure of the brief.

Include one example of proof you are willing to show. A public project with a constraint is enough. If your proof is private, describe the constraint anyway, even if the name stays off the site. The layout needs something true to hold.

Say what done is. The sentences live on the real pages. A past customer recognizes the company. A new visitor can tell what to do. The retired pages do not rank ahead of the new ones because nobody set a redirect. Titles match the visible headings.

On a Hanabi project the build follows that brief. The studio designs and builds, so the sentences are not a document that dies in a slide. They end up in the site, in a repo the client owns, with brand files and notes in the client portal after delivery.

## How not to pay for both at once

Do not ask for a visual exploration "to see what happens" while the offer is unstable. You will fall in love with a direction for a company you have not decided to be. Explorations are cheap only when they are disposable. They stop being disposable the moment a founder shows them to a board.

Do not keep the old navigation "for now" if the offer changed. The navigation is the offer, in short form. Old labels will pull the new sentences back into the old business.

Do not launch the new look on the homepage and leave the product, the proposal template, and the invoice in the old voice. Those are the pages where trust is confirmed or lost. A redesign of the marketing site that does not reach the first email is a costume.

If you are unsure which fork you are on, say the offer in one sentence and ask a customer to correct it. Their correction is the brief. A workshop that never speaks to a customer will produce a more articulate version of your internal confusion.

Once the sentences are true, the next risk is shipping them without looking at the real pages. The piece on [design QA before a site goes live](/blog/design-qa-before-a-site-goes-live) is the next read, so the new understanding survives contact with a phone, a form, and the type you will actually render.

When the fork is the thing you need to settle with a studio, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The useful question to bring is whether you are clarifying an offer or replacing one. The work starts there.
